Chinese Crested Skin, Dental, and Temperature Planning

Plan Chinese Crested care around bare-skin protection, temperature comfort, small-breed dental needs, and a worksheet you fill with local quotes.

Published: 2026-10-22Sources checked: 3Educational planning guide

The Chinese Crested's defining feature, exposed skin on the hairless variety, drives its care plan, so ownership is mostly about sun and temperature protection, a small-breed dental routine, and gentle daily habits.

Why this breed needs a different plan

The American Kennel Club describes the Chinese Crested as a sweet, slender, ultra-affectionate companion with spotted pink skin, a spiky crest, furry socks, and a feathery tail, and calls it truly a breed apart. The hairless variety leaves much of the skin exposed, and there is also a coated powderpuff variety. That exposed skin, more than anything else, shapes daily care.

The core answer: plan for skin protection, temperature comfort, and gentle grooming rather than heavy coat work, and start dental care early because small breeds need it. This guide gives a worksheet and daily habits, and pairs with our five-year ownership cost framework and hairless breed skin care budget.

Protecting exposed skin

The Merck Veterinary Manual explains that the skin is the body's largest organ and that a normal hair coat helps protect the skin from physical and ultraviolet light damage and helps regulate body temperature; it also notes that melanin, the skin's pigment, helps protect cells from the sun's damaging rays. A hairless dog simply has less of that natural protection over much of its body.

The practical takeaway is to reduce harsh sun exposure, keep the skin clean and moisturized per your vet's guidance, and watch for irritation. Ask your veterinarian which skin-care products and any sun protection are appropriate rather than guessing, and use our skin care cost buffer guide to leave room in the budget for unexpected skin needs.

Merck also explains that the epidermis, the outer layer, constantly renews itself and that oil glands produce sebum, which keeps skin soft and pliable and gives a coat its sheen. On a largely hairless dog, that natural oil is more visible and the skin is more directly exposed to the environment, which is why gentle, regular cleaning and observation become part of the routine. Get in the habit of running your hands over the skin during quiet moments so you notice changes early and can raise them with your vet before they become bigger problems.

Warmth and temperature comfort

Merck notes that a normal coat helps conserve heat by trapping air and that the hair coat also helps regulate body temperature. A hairless dog has less insulation, so it may feel cold more readily and appreciate a sweater in cool conditions and a warm resting spot indoors. In strong sun or heat, shade and water matter for any dog. Do not improvise around extremes; ask your vet what temperature precautions fit your individual dog, and see our cold-weather breed fit guide for how to think about seasonal comfort.

A little planning makes this easy rather than burdensome. Keep a couple of well-fitting sweaters on hand for cool mornings, choose a draft-free spot for the dog's bed, and pay attention to your dog's own signals: seeking warmth, shivering, or reluctance to go outside in the cold are worth heeding. The coated powderpuff variety has more natural covering than the hairless variety, so if temperature management feels daunting, that difference between the two coat types is worth discussing with a breeder or your vet.

A small-breed dental routine

The Merck Veterinary Manual notes that periodontal disease is the leading cause of tooth loss in dogs and that small-breed dogs tend to have more problems with it than large breeds. Merck also notes that some small breeds are prone to teeth that fail to erupt normally, which is why it recommends veterinary examination. The good news is that Merck states gum disease will not develop around clean teeth and recommends home care such as daily brushing with canine, not human, toothpaste plus regular veterinary exams.

Start a gentle home routine early and ask your vet how often professional cleaning is right for your dog; our dental cleaning budget questions help you plan for it.

Skin-and-dental cost worksheet

BucketFormula to fill
SetupSweaters or coats + vet-recommended skin products + toothbrush and canine paste + small crate
MonthlyFood (small-breed portion) + parasite prevention quote + skin-care and wipe supplies
Annual(Monthly x 12) + wellness exam + vaccines quote + budget line for veterinary dental care
Skin reserveBuffer for unexpected skin irritation visits or products your vet recommends
ReserveGeneral emergency fund target you can maintain

Because skin needs are individual, treat the skin reserve as a distinct line rather than folding it into general costs.

A one-week care test

  1. Skin check habit: Practice a daily two-minute skin inspection routine and note whether you kept it up.
  2. Temperature awareness: Track indoor and outdoor temperatures and plan when a sweater or shade would be needed.
  3. Tooth handling: Rehearse the daily-brushing habit Merck recommends so a real dog accepts it calmly.
  4. Sun planning: Map the sunniest hours of your day and how you would limit harsh exposure.

If the daily attention felt easy, this affectionate little dog can be a lovely fit; if not, reconsider the commitment.

Questions for a breeder, rescue, or vet

The Orthopedic Foundation for Animals notes that a CHIC certification reflects that a dog completed its parent club's recommended screenings and shared the results publicly, not that results were all normal.

  • Which screenings does the breed club recommend, and can I see the parents' records?
  • For the hairless variety, what skin-care routine do you follow, and how do the dogs handle sun and cold?
  • For a rescue: is there any history of skin irritation or dental problems?
  • For your vet: what skin products, sun precautions, and dental schedule fit this dog?

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Treating bare skin like a coat. It needs protection Merck attributes to a normal hair coat, including from ultraviolet light.
  • Ignoring temperature. Less insulation means more attention to warmth and to shade and water in heat.
  • Delaying dental care. Merck flags small breeds as prone to periodontal disease; start home care early.
  • Guessing at products. Ask your vet before applying skin or sun products.

Finally, do not assume less hair means less care overall. It simply shifts the work from coat maintenance to skin, temperature, and dental attention, which are steady daily habits rather than occasional big tasks.

What this guide cannot tell you

It cannot recommend a specific skin product, sunscreen, or temperature threshold for your individual dog, and it cannot diagnose or treat skin or dental conditions. Merck's information is general education. Only your veterinarian can examine your dog's skin and mouth and tell you what care, products, and precautions are appropriate. Use this to build habits and a budget, then confirm every specific with your vet and local providers.

FAQ

Does a hairless Chinese Crested need sun protection?
Its exposed skin lacks the natural protection Merck attributes to a normal hair coat, which includes shielding from ultraviolet light. That means limiting harsh sun exposure and asking your veterinarian which skin-care or sun-protection products are appropriate. Do not apply human products by assumption; your vet can recommend what suits your individual dog and its skin.
Do these dogs get cold easily?
They can. Merck notes that a normal coat helps conserve body heat by trapping air, so a largely hairless dog has less insulation and may feel cold sooner. A sweater in cool weather and a warm indoor resting spot help. In heat, shade and water matter as for any dog. Ask your vet about precautions that fit your dog and climate.
Is dental care a big deal for this breed?
Yes. The Merck Veterinary Manual notes that periodontal disease is the leading cause of tooth loss in dogs and that small breeds are especially prone, and it says gum disease will not develop around clean teeth. Start a gentle home routine such as daily brushing with canine toothpaste early, and ask your vet how often professional cleaning is appropriate.
